analysis.one_liner: Blocks OSHA from issuing its first federal rule protecting workers from extreme heat.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop OSHA's proposed heat-safety standard, introduced by Senator Cassidy with 12 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Senate health and labor committee and has received no hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: OSHA proposed the first nationwide standard requiring employers to protect workers from heat, including water, rest breaks, shade, and written heat-safety plans [S2]. This bill would legally forbid the Labor Department from finalizing, carrying out, or enforcing that proposal — or anything substantially like it [S2]. It was introduced in late April 2026 and sent to the Senate HELP Committee, where it has sat without action [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers in heat-exposed industries — agriculture, construction, warehousing, delivery, and other outdoor and hot-indoor work — would avoid the costs of the proposed rule: providing drinking water, shade or cooling areas, rest breaks, acclimatization plans for new workers, and written heat-safety plans. The bill's own findings argue these requirements are 'overly prescriptive' and 'burdensome to businesses' [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Secretary of Labor from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the proposed 'Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings' standard published in the Federal Register on August 30, 2024, or any substantially similar standard [S2].

States Congress's findings that the proposed standard's prescriptive requirements — high-heat triggers, mandated rest-break protocols, acclimatization protocols, and detailed written safety plans — are 'overly prescriptive, burdensome to businesses, and confusing for workers' [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Outdoor and hot-indoor workers — farm crews, construction workers, warehouse and delivery workers, and others — would go without the first federal rule requiring employers to provide water, rest breaks, shade or cooling, and heat-safety planning. The bill covers all industries and all climates with no substitute protections [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves workers in heat-exposed jobs with no federal heat-safety protections and prohibits not just this specific rule but 'any substantially similar standard,' foreclosing a narrower rewrite [S2].

The bill's findings concede the rule covers 'all industries and geographies'; the honest objection it raises is that prescriptive triggers, rest-break protocols, and written plans may not fit every workplace and climate, imposing compliance costs on small employers in cooler regions where heat exposure differs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Employers get relief from compliance costs; workers in the hottest jobs get nothing in return — no substitute protections are offered, and the ban extends to any similar future rule. The strongest point on the bill's side is that a single prescriptive standard may fit rice fields and Minnesota warehouses poorly, but the bill doesn't fix that; it simply bans the standard outright.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced April 29, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Cassidy (R-LA) introduced the bill on April 29, 2026, joined by eight original cosponsors including Senators Risch, Tuberville, Crapo, Budd, Daines, Sheehy, Cornyn, and Tillis [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the full action history shows no further steps [S4].
The bill targets the OSHA proposed rule 'Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings' published August 30, 2024 (89 Fed. Reg. 70698) [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, heat-exposed employers — the bill's beneficiaries — are better off: the bill's stall means no law has blocked the rule, but no federal heat standard has been finalized either, so employers continue operating without the proposed water, rest-break, shade, and written-plan requirements while workers remain uncovered.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar the Labor Department from finalizing or enforcing the proposed OSHA heat standard [S2, S4].

for.name: 12 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 12 cosponsors were Republicans, including original cosponsors Risch, Tuberville, Crapo, Budd, Daines, Sheehy, Cornyn, and Tillis [S3].

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S4].

against.name: Occupational Safety and Health Administration
against.what_they_did: Published the proposed heat-safety standard the bill would prohibit, whose rulemaking this bill is designed to stop [S2].

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors are Republicans; no Democrats have signed on, and the bill has drawn no recorded floor activity [S3].

industries.note: Farm crews face some of the highest heat exposure of any workforce; the bill would spare these employers the proposed rule's water, shade, rest-break, and acclimatization requirements, with the cost borne by the workers left unprotected [S2].
Roofers, road crews, and other outdoor trades would avoid compliance costs for water, rest breaks, and heat-safety plans; their workers would forgo the protections [S2].
The proposed rule covers indoor heat as well as outdoor; blocking it spares warehouses and delivery operations cooling and rest-break mandates, leaving workers in hot indoor settings uncovered [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill has received no committee action and no bipartisan cosponsors, so it is very likely to die quietly when this Congress ends. The more realistic threat to the heat rule runs outside this bill — through the agency's own rulemaking pace or appropriations language — rather than through this standalone measure.
